extra.message: GET /api/search passes the attacker-controlled searchTerm directly to res.send(). String responses use HTML content type, so a crafted URL containing script markup executes JavaScript when a victim visits it.

The URL fragment is automatically submitted as a search term at lines 18–20. The server echoes it, and $sce.trustAsHtml(response) bypasses sanitization before xss-search.html:18 inserts it using ng-bind-html. A crafted /xss-search fragment therefore executes attacker-controlled HTML event handlers in the victim's browser.

POST /api/user/profile stores req.body unchanged in src/server/routes.js:45. When that profile is retrieved, its lastName is trusted as HTML and rendered through ng-bind-html in csrf.html:32. An attacker can store malicious markup through the unprotected profile endpoint and execute JavaScript when another user retrieves the affected profile.

POST /api/user/login issues a userAuthToken and initializes the shared user profile without checking credentials or any identity proof. Any unauthenticated caller obtains the token accepted by the profile read and update handlers. Those handlers also lack session validation and use the supplied cookie directly as the profile key.

cwe: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function

extra.message: The generated value is overwritten with the fixed authentication token '35592211433686316'. Every login shares this token and profile. An attacker can supply this known cookie to read or overwrite an initialized user's profile without possessing that user's session. This credential is embedded in the demonstration application.

The profile update relies on an automatically attached cookie and accepts form submissions without checking a CSRF token or request origin. src/server/app.js:17 enables URL-encoded bodies. The form in attacker-app/src/client/app/csrf-attack/csrf-attack.html:10–14 submits attacker-selected profile fields from another origin; the documented localhost ports are same-site, so SameSite defaults do not prevent this attack.

Logout clears the browser cookie and data.randomNumber, but retains data.profile[token]. Profile handlers consult only the supplied cookie and never check data.randomNumber or an expiration timestamp. Replaying a saved token therefore permits profile access after logout or after the cookie's one-hour lifetime.
The userAuthToken cookie is issued without httpOnly, making the authentication cookie readable through document.cookie. The confirmed search and profile XSS vulnerabilities can therefore extract it.

The authentication cookie is issued without secure, allowing browsers to transmit it over unencrypted HTTP. The application directly serves HTTP, so network observers can capture the token when it is accessed over an observable network connection.

extra.message: An unauthenticated caller controls both the userAuthToken dictionary key and the stored request body. extra.message: data.profile is an ordinary object, and the attacker-controlled cookie is used as an unrestricted property name. Supplying userAuthToken=__proto__ assigns req.body as the shared profile dictionary's prototype. Subsequent profile reads at line 35 include inherited properties, allowing attacker-injected prototype entries to be returned as profiles for keys without an own entry. This mutates the shared dictionary's prototype, not the global Object.prototype.
